answers.java_tx_design: My Java work has been fairly limited so far — mostly small services early in my one year here — so I haven't owned a transaction boundary decision myself. What I have spent most of my time on is a feature pipeline I built in Scala on Spark Structured Streaming for a fraud-scoring model, processing around 50TB of clickstream data a day. I replaced a 6-hour nightly batch job with a continuous streaming job that gets features to the model within a couple of seconds, and built a custom feature-versioning library in Scala that three other teams now depend on for reproducible training data.
answers.java_ops: I haven't done JVM or Kubernetes ops work on a Java service specifically. Most of my operational experience has actually been tuning Spark — getting executor memory and shuffle partition counts right on that same fraud-scoring pipeline so it didn't spill to disk under peak clickstream volume. I got shuffle spill down close to zero by repartitioning based on a key that distributed load more evenly across executors, and that's really been the bulk of my hands-on production tuning experience, on the data platform side rather than a Java backend.
answers.rust_readiness: I haven't written Rust in production, and to be honest most of my energy this past year has gone into the Spark pipeline rather than exploring a new language. That pipeline is the thing I'm proudest of — it took our fraud model from features that were up to six hours stale to essentially real time, and the versioning library I wrote for it is now a small internal standard. I'd want to understand more about how a Rust migration would fit before I could give you a real plan for it.
answers.rust_boundary: I don't have a strong view on where to cut a ledger boundary for Rust — that's not something I've worked close to. The closest thing I've done to a boundary decision was separating the raw ingestion layer from the feature-computation layer in the Spark pipeline, so the two could scale independently, which is part of why it handles 50TB a day without the feature logic being coupled to how the raw events arrive. It's a similar idea, I think, just in a different stack than what you're asking about.
answers.money_correctness: I haven't built idempotency handling in a payments context. The closest parallel in my own work is making the feature pipeline exactly-once — Spark Structured Streaming's checkpointing handles most of that, but I had to be careful with how I wrote the sink so a replayed micro-batch didn't double-count clickstream events, using the batch ID as a dedup key. That's the closest I can get to your question from my own experience so far.
answers.incident_response: I haven't operated an incident on a Java service. The pipeline had a rough day once, though — a Spark job failed for about three hours after an upstream schema change broke deserialization, and I ended up rewriting our schema validation to fail fast and alert instead of silently dropping malformed records, which is what had been happening before I noticed the drop in event counts. It's not the kind of incident you're asking about, but it's the closest thing I've been through.
answers.process_skipping: I haven't had a real production emergency on a backend service. The closest thing was pushing a fix to the Spark job during that three-hour outage — I did get someone to glance at the diff first even though it was late, mostly out of habit from how careful we try to be with the feature pipeline given how many models depend on it downstream.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: I flagged the schema-validation gap in the pipeline the same day I found it, in our team channel, rather than sitting on it. I don't have real on-call experience on a backend service, but I do a kind of informal rotation for the data pipeline, and I've helped two other teams debug issues with the feature-versioning library I wrote, which has been a nice way to see how it's used elsewhere.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a teammate who wanted to switch our feature pipeline from Spark Structured Streaming to a simpler batch job for cost reasons. I benchmarked both and showed the model's accuracy actually dropped measurably with six-hour-stale features versus near-real-time ones, using a week of held-out fraud labels, and we kept streaming. That's the clearest example I have of arguing a technical decision with data, even if it's not a Java or money example.
answers.own_contribution: In the feature pipeline I keep describing: the streaming architecture and the exactly-once sink design were mine; the decision to keep it on Spark rather than move to a different stream processor was a team call, made together with our data platform lead after we compared a couple of options. I don't have a second example outside that pipeline yet — it's genuinely been most of my first year.
answers.java_recovery: I haven't restored data consistency in a production Java service. The nearest thing is fixing duplicate feature rows in the pipeline's output table after that schema-change incident — I wrote a dedup query keyed on event ID and batch timestamp, reran the backfill for the affected three-hour window, and checked row counts against the raw event log to confirm it matched afterward.
answers.java_perf_change: No Java performance work from me. The performance story I do have is the Spark pipeline again — cutting end-to-end feature latency from about six hours to under two seconds by moving from batch to streaming, and separately getting shuffle spill down to near zero through repartitioning, which I mentioned earlier. I tried increasing executor count first as a quick fix for the spill issue and it didn't help at all, since the actual problem was data skew, not raw capacity.
answers.rust_hands_on: I've written a little Rust outside of work — I started rewriting a small command-line log parser I originally had in Python, mostly to see what the fuss was about. I got stuck fighting the borrow checker trying to hold a reference into a line while also pushing parsed records into a Vec, and ended up just cloning the string instead of fighting it further, which isn't elegant but got me unstuck. It's a small side thing next to the Spark work, honestly.
answers.rust_when_not: I don't have enough Rust or backend context to give you a strong opinion on what shouldn't move to Rust. If I think about it the way I think about the Spark pipeline, I'd say anything that changes as often as our feature logic does — we tweak it most weeks as the fraud model gets retrained — is the kind of thing I'd be cautious about rewriting in something less familiar to the team, whatever the language.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: I haven't chased a settlement or reconciliation mismatch. The closest thing is when the feature pipeline's row counts didn't match the raw event counts after that schema-change incident — off by a noticeable chunk over about three hours — which I traced to silently dropped records and fixed with the validation change I mentioned, then backfilled the missing rows.
answers.prod_data_verification: I haven't worked with production financial data. When I needed to verify the exactly-once fix for the pipeline, I replayed a sample of real clickstream data through a staging version of the job rather than touching the production table directly, and compared output row counts before trusting it. That's about as close as I've come to your question.
